title: Water Equivalent (W) — Definition & Derivation
notes: **Definition of water equivalent $W$:** The mass of water that would require the same amount of heat as a given body to raise its temperature by $1^\circ\text{C}$ (or 1 K). It is the **thermal capacity of the body expressed in mass units of water**.

**Thermal capacity (heat capacity):** $C = mc$ — the heat required to raise the temperature of a body by $1^\circ\text{C}$. Water equivalent $W$ is defined so that $W \times c_w = m \times c$, therefore **$W = \frac{m \cdot c}{c_w}$**, where $c_w = 4200\text{ J/kg·K}$ or $1\text{ cal/g·°C}$.

**Physical meaning:** A calorimeter with water equivalent $W = 20\text{ g}$ absorbs as much heat when warming by $1^\circ\text{C}$ as 20 g of water. The calorimeter's own mass $m_{cal}$ and its specific heat $c_{cal}$ contribute: $W = \frac{m_{cal} c_{cal}}{c_w}$.

**Derivation:** For a body of mass $m$, specific heat $c$, raising temperature by $\Delta T$: heat gained $H = mc\Delta T$. For $W$ grams of water gaining same heat: $H = W \cdot c_w \cdot \Delta T$. Equating: $mc\Delta T = W c_w \Delta T \Rightarrow W = \frac{mc}{c_w}$.
**Units:** Since $c$ has units $\text{J/kg·K}$ or $\text{cal/g·°C}$, and $m$ has kg or g, $W$ has units of **kg** or **g** (mass). Note: $W$ is not a heat capacity itself — it is a mass equivalent.

**For calorimeter:** $W_{cal} = \frac{m_{cal} c_{cal}}{c_w}$. For thin copper calorimeter: $c_{Cu} \approx 390\text{ J/kg·K}$, $c_w = 4186\text{ J/kg·K}$, so $W_{Cu} \approx 0.093 m_{Cu}$. A 50 g copper calorimeter has $W \approx 4.7\text{ g}$.

**Why water as reference?** Water has the highest specific heat of common liquids ($c_w = 4186\text{ J/kg·K}$ at $20^\circ\text{C}$). Using water as the reference makes $W$ directly comparable to actual water mass — physical meaning is intuitive.

**Effective heat capacity in calorimetry:** When a calorimeter contains liquid of mass $m_l$, specific heat $c_l$, and water equivalent $W$, the total effective heat capacity is $C_{eff} = m_l c_l + W c_w$. This is used in both method of mixtures and method of cooling.
**In method of cooling:** Formula $(m_1 c_1 + W c_w)/t_1 = (m_2 c_2 + W c_w)/t_2$ accounts for calorimeter heat capacity. If $W$ is neglected, calculated $c_2$ has systematic error.

**Finding $W$ experimentally:** (1) Cool known mass of water from $T_1$ to $T_2$, measure time $t_1$. (2) Cool same calorimeter with different mass of water, measure $t_2$. (3) Solve two equations: $(m_1 c_w + W c_w)/t_1 = (m_2 c_w + W c_w)/t_2$. This eliminates $k$ and gives $W$.
**NEB exam focus:** Define $W$, derive $W = mc/c_w$, calculate $W$ for given calorimeter, include $W$ in calorimetry equations, distinguish between water equivalent and actual mass of calorimeter.

**Connection to heat capacity:** Heat capacity $C = mc$. Since $c_w = 1\text{ cal/g·°C}$ in CGS, $W = mc$ numerically equals the heat capacity in calories per degree. For any body in SI: $C = W \times 4.2\text{ J/°C}$.

**Applications:** Calorimetry (all types),热水器 design ($W$ concept used in thermal mass calculations), building thermal mass ($W$ of walls/furniture affects room temperature stability), spacecraft thermal control.

**Special cases:** For ideal gas in bomb calorimeter (constant volume): $C_V$ used instead of $c$. For phase change calorimetry: effective $W$ includes latent heat contributions. For food calorimetry: $W$ of bomb calorimeter includes ignition wire, crucible.
confusion: Water equivalent $W$ is the mass of water in the calorimeter — $W$ is a **calculated mass-equivalent**, not actual water present. For a dry copper calorimeter of mass 50 g, $W \approx 4.7\text{ g}$. No water is inside.

Water equivalent and heat capacity are the same thing — Heat capacity $C = mc$ has units $\text{J/°C}$. Water equivalent $W = mc/c_w$ has units of **mass** (g or kg). They are related by $C = W \times c_w$, but numerically different in SI.

The water equivalent of a calorimeter is constant — $W = m_{cal} c_{cal}/c_w$. Since $c_w$ is nearly constant, $W$ is constant for a given calorimeter. But $c_w$ itself varies with temperature ($4.186\to4.219\text{ J/g·K}$), so $W$ varies slightly.

A heavier calorimeter always has larger $W$ — Not always. $W \propto m \times c_{cal}$. Aluminum ($c \approx 900$) has higher specific heat per unit mass than copper ($c \approx 390$). So an aluminum calorimeter has **higher $W$ per unit mass** than copper.

Water equivalent is used only in method of cooling — $W$ appears in **all calorimetry calculations**: method of mixtures, method of cooling, bomb calorimetry, and steam calorimetry. Any time a calorimeter absorbs heat, $W$ must be included.

The formula $W = mc/c_w$ means the body behaves like $mc/c_w$ grams of water — **Yes, this is exactly the physical meaning.** A 100 g copper block ($c = 390$) has $W = 100\times390/4186 = 9.3\text{ g}$ — it behaves thermally like 9.3 g of water.

Water equivalent can be negative — $W$ is always positive since $m > 0$, $c > 0$, $c_w > 0$. However, in some contexts (endothermic reactions in calorimeter) the effective $W$ from calibration includes correction factors.

All calorimeters have negligible $W$ — Thin copper calorimeters have small $W \approx 0.1 m$. But thick brass calorimeters, massive aluminum blocks, or calorimeters with large stirrers can have $W$ comparable to liquid mass ($\sim 20\%\text{--}50\%$ of liquid mass).

Water equivalent is independent of temperature — $c_w$ varies by $\sim 1\%$ from $0^\circ\text{C}$ to $100^\circ\text{C}$. For precise work, use $c_w$ at the **average temperature** of the experiment. In school physics, $4.2\text{ J/g·K}$ is standard.

Water equivalent is measured in liters — Since density of water $\approx 1\text{ g/mL}$, $1000\text{ g} = 1\text{ L}$. But $W$ is defined in **mass units**, not volume. A $W = 50\text{ g}$ means thermal capacity equivalent to 50 mL of water.
practice: A copper calorimeter weighs 60 g. Specific heat of copper $= 390\text{ J/kg·K}$. Find its water equivalent. If filled with 150 g of water, what is total effective thermal capacity? [Solution: $W_{cal} = m_{cal}c_{cal}/c_w = 0.06 \times 390 / 4186 = 0.00559\text{ kg} = 5.59\text{ g}$. Total $C_{eff} = m_w c_w + W c_w = (150 + 5.59) \times 4.186 = 651.3\text{ J/°C}$ or $C_{eff} = m_l c_l + W_{cal}c_w = 150\times4.186 + 5.59\times4.186 = 651.3\text{ J/°C}$.]

A calorimeter of water equivalent 12 g contains 80 g of water at $20^\circ\text{C}$. A hot metal piece (mass 50 g, $c = 400\text{ J/kg·K}$) at $100^\circ\text{C}$ is dropped in. Find final equilibrium temperature. [Solution: Heat lost by metal = heat gained by water + calorimeter. $50\times0.4\times(100-T) = (80+12)\times4.2\times(T-20)$. $20(100-T) = 92\times4.2\times(T-20)$. $2000-20T = 386.4T - 7728$. $406.4T = 9728 \Rightarrow T = 23.94^\circ\text{C}$.]

Two calorimeters A and B have water equivalents $W_A = 8\text{ g}$ and $W_B = 15\text{ g}$. Both contain 100 g of water at $25^\circ\text{C}$. Equal masses (50 g) of a hot substance ($c = 2000\text{ J/kg·K}$) at $100^\circ\text{C}$ are added to each. Will final temperatures differ? [Solution: A: effective mass $= 100+8 = 108\text{ g}$. B: $100+15 = 115\text{ g}$. $50\times2(100-T_A) = 108\times4.2\times(T_A-25) \Rightarrow T_A = 36.5^\circ\text{C}$. B: $100-T_B = 115\times2.1\times(T_B-25)/50 \Rightarrow T_B = 35.8^\circ\circ\text{C}$. Yes, B has slightly lower final $T$ because larger $W$ absorbs more heat.]

How would you determine the water equivalent of a calorimeter experimentally using the method of cooling? [Solution: (1) Fill calorimeter with mass $m_1$ of water, cool from $T_1$ to $T_2$, record time $t_1$. (2) Repeat with mass $m_2$ of water, same $T_1\to T_2$, record $t_2$. (3) Method of cooling: $(m_1c_w + Wc_w)/t_1 = (m_2c_w + Wc_w)/t_2$. (4) Solve: $W = c_w(m_2 t_1 - m_1 t_2)/(t_1 - t_2)$.]

A calorimeter of mass 100 g and $c = 900\text{ J/kg·K}$ is used. Calculate $W$. Compare with a copper calorimeter of same mass ($c = 390\text{ J/kg·K}$). [Solution: Aluminum: $W_{Al} = 100\times900/4186 = 21.5\text{ g}$. Copper: $W_{Cu} = 100\times390/4186 = 9.3\text{ g}$. Same mass, aluminum has $W$ 2.3× larger because $c_{Al} > c_{Cu}$.]

In a method of cooling experiment, the formula $\frac{(m_1 + W)c_w}{t_1} = \frac{(m_2 + W)c_w}{t_2}$ is used. If $m_1 = 100\text{ g}$, $m_2 = 120\text{ g}$, $t_1 = 5\text{ min}$, $t_2 = 4\text{ min}$, find $W$. [Solution: $(100+W)/5 = (120+W)/4 \Rightarrow 4(100+W) = 5(120+W) \Rightarrow 400 + 4W = 600 + 5W \Rightarrow W = -200\text{ g}$. Negative $W$ is physically impossible — indicates experimental error, non-Newtonian cooling, or wrong assumptions. Recheck measurements.]

Steam at $100^\circ\text{C}$ is passed into a calorimeter of water equivalent 15 g containing 200 g of water at $20^\circ\text{C}$. The mass of condensed steam is 5 g. Find final temperature. (Latent heat of steam $L = 540\text{ cal/g}$.) [Solution: Heat from condensing steam: $5 \times 540 = 2700\text{ cal}$. Heat from cooling condensed water ($100\to T$): $5\times(100-T)\text{ cal}$. Heat gained by water + calorimeter: $(200+15)(T-20)\text{ cal}$. $2700 + 5(100-T) = 215(T-20) \Rightarrow 2700 + 500 - 5T = 215T - 4300 \Rightarrow 220T = 7500 \Rightarrow T = 34.1^\circ\text{C}$.]

A calorimeter with stirrer ($W = 10\text{ g}$) contains 150 g of water at $15^\circ\text{C}$. When 100 g of a substance at $80^\circ\text{C}$ ($c = 800\text{ J/kg·K}$) is added, equilibrium is $25^\circ\text{C}$. Find $W$ again using this data. [Solution: Heat lost by substance: $0.1 \times 800 \times 55 = 4400\text{ J}$. Heat gained by water+calorimeter: $(0.15\times4200 + W\times4200)(10) = (630 + 4200W) \times 10 = 6300 + 42000W\text{ J}$. $4400 = 6300 + 42000W \Rightarrow W = -0.0452\text{ kg} = -45.2\text{ g}$. Negative! Suggests heat loss to surroundings, incomplete mixing, or wrong $c$.]

State the physical meaning of water equivalent. A calorimeter of mass 80 g has water equivalent 7.5 g. Find specific heat of calorimeter material. [Solution: Physical meaning: The mass of water that would absorb the same heat as the calorimeter for the same temperature rise. $W = m_{cal}c_{cal}/c_w \Rightarrow 7.5 = 80 \times c_{cal} / 4.2 \Rightarrow c_{cal} = 7.5 \times 4.2 / 80 = 0.394\text{ J/g·K} = 394\text{ J/kg·K}$. Material is likely copper or brass.]

Two calorimeters of water equivalents $W_1 = 10\text{ g}$ and $W_2 = 20\text{ g}$ contain equal masses of water. The same hot solid is added to each. Show that the temperature rise is inversely proportional to $(m + W)$. [Solution: Heat lost by solid $Q = m_s c_s (T_s - T)$. Heat gained: $Q = (m_w + W)c_w (T - T_i)$. $T - T_i = \frac{m_s c_s}{c_w(m_w + W)}(T_s - T)$. Since $m_s, c_s, T_s, T$ are same for both, $(T - T_i)(m_w + W) = \text{constant}$. Thus $(T - T_i) \propto 1/(m_w + W)$. Larger $W$ → smaller $\Delta T$.]
universalFacts: Historical: The concept of water equivalent was introduced by **Joseph Black** (1760s), who coined 'latent heat' and made precise calorimetry measurements. Black's water equivalent was the basis for the calorie definition — 1 calorie = heat to raise 1 g of water by $1^\circ\text{C}$.

The calorie (cal) is defined relative to water: **1 cal = heat to raise 1 g of water by $1^\circ\text{C}$ at $14.5^\circ\text{C}$**. This makes $c_w = 1\text{ cal/g·°C}$ by definition. In SI, $1\text{ cal} = 4.184\text{ J}$ (thermochemical), $4.1868\text{ J}$ (international).

NEB exam tip: Many calorimetry problems in NEB give $W$ directly. If not given and calorimeter is mentioned, **assume $W$ is negligible** unless specified otherwise, or estimate $W \approx 0.1 m_{cal}$ for thin copper calorimeter.

Real-world: **Solar thermal systems** use water equivalent to size thermal storage tanks. The thermal mass of a building (walls, furniture, water) is expressed as 'liters of water equivalent' — how many liters of water would provide the same temperature stability.

Connection to specific heat: Materials with **high specific heat** (water, concrete, brick) have large $W$ per unit mass. This is why coastal climates are milder — water's high $c$ moderates temperature. Desert sand has low $c \approx 800\text{ J/kg·K}$, causing extreme day/night swings.

Calorimeter materials: **Copper** ($c \approx 390$) has low $W$ per unit mass — ideal for sensitive calorimetry. **Aluminum** ($c \approx 900$) has moderate $W$. **Glass** ($c \approx 800$) has higher $W$. Stainless steel ($c \approx 500$) is common for lab calorimeters.

Advanced: **Mixing calorimeters** use the method of mixtures with $W$ correction. **Bomb calorimeters** (constant volume) use $C_V$ instead of $c_p$. **Adiabatic calorimeters** minimize heat loss (effectively $W$ of surroundings = 0). **Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC)** measures $W$ and phase changes precisely.

NEB practical tip: In the calorimetry practical, always tabulate: mass of empty calorimeter ($m_1$), mass with water ($m_2$), mass of water ($m_w = m_2 - m_1$), mass of unknown solid/liquid, initial temperatures, final temperature. Calculate heat gained and lost, then $c$.
